On images of affine spacesThanks: Supported by the grant RSF-DST 22-41-02019

Ivan Arzhantsev Address: Faculty of Computer Science, HSE University, Pokrovsky Boulevard 11, Moscow, 109028 Russia Email address: arjantsev@hse.ru
Abstract.

We prove that every non-degenerate toric variety, every homogeneous space of a connected linear algebraic group without non-constant invertible regular functions, and every variety covered by affine spaces admits a surjective morphism from an affine space.

Key words and phrases:
Affine space, morphism, image, unirational variety, invertible function, flexible variety, toric variety, homogeneous space
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 14A10, 14R10 Secondary 14M20, 14M22

1. AA-images and very flexible varieties

There is no doubt that the affine spaces 𝔸m\mathbb{A}^{m} play the key role in mathematics and other fields of science. It is all the more surprising that despite the centuries-old history of study, to this day a number of natural and even naive questions about affine spaces remain open. Here we can mention the Jacobian conjecture, the cancellation problem, the linearization problem, the problem of recognition of tame and wild automorphisms, and a number of other unsolved problems. The question of which varieties can be realized as images of morphisms from an affine space to other varieties also seems nontrivial. The purpose of this note is to show that the class of such images is surprisingly wide and entirely includes several important classes of algebraic varieties. Our results are based on the theory of flexible varieties developed in [2] and subsequent works, and on a canonical quotient realization of a variety coming from the theory of Cox rings, see [6, 1].

Below we consider algebraic varieties over an algebraically closed field 𝕂\mathbb{K} of characteristic zero.

Definition 1.

An algebraic variety XX is called an AA-image if for some positive integer mm there is a surjective morphism φ:𝔸m→X\varphi\colon\mathbb{A}^{m}\to X.

Clearly, every AA-image is irreducible. Moreover, if ff is an invertible regular function on XX, the pull-back function φ∗​(f)\varphi^{*}(f) is an invertible regular function on 𝔸m\mathbb{A}^{m}. This proves that every invertible regular function on an AA-image is constant. Finally, let us recall that an irreducible algebraic variety XX is unirational if the field of rational functions 𝕂⁡(X)\mathbb{K}(X) can be embedded in a purely transcendental extension 𝕂⁡(x1,…,xm)\mathbb{K}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}) of the ground field 𝕂\mathbb{K}, or, equivalently, there exists a rational dominant morphism from some affine space 𝔸m\mathbb{A}^{m} to XX. It follows that every AA-image is a unirational variety. Honestly speaking, we have no example of a unirational variety without non-constant invertible regular functions which is not an AA-image. Moreover, explicit computations show that many varieties from this class can be realized as images of affine spaces.

Example 1.

There is a surjective morphism φ:𝔸1→ℙ1\varphi\colon\mathbb{A}^{1}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}. It can be given, for example, by

x→[1+x2:x].x\to[1+x^{2}:x].
Example 2.

It is easy to check that the image of the morphism 𝔸2→𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}\to\mathbb{A}^{2} given by

(x,y)→(1+x​y,x+y2+x​y3)(x,y)\to(1+xy,x+y^{2}+xy^{3})

is 𝔸2∖{0}\mathbb{A}^{2}\setminus\{0\}. So we obtain a surjective morphism φ:𝔸2→𝔸2∖{0}\varphi\colon\mathbb{A}^{2}\to\mathbb{A}^{2}\setminus\{0\}. Let us note that in [20, Section 1] the authors were interested in the existence of such a morphism.

Remark 1.

As we learned from [5], Zbigniew Jelonek has constructed such and more general examples much earlier, see [14]. In [5, Proposition 1.5], one may find an explicit formulas for a morphism ℂn→ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n}, n≥2n\geq 2, such that the complement of the image is a given finite set of points.

Since there is a quotient morphism 𝔸2∖{0}→ℙ1\mathbb{A}^{2}\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}, Example 2 provides one more way to obtain the projective line ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} as an image of affine space. In the present note we generalize this approach in order to obtain many varieties as AA-images.

Let us proceed with the following obvious observations.

Lemma 1.
  1. a)

    If ψ:X1→X2\psi\colon X_{1}\to X_{2} is a surjective morphism of algebraic varieties and X1X_{1} is an AA-image, then X2X_{2} is an AA-image.

  2. b)

    If X1X_{1} and X2X_{2} are AA-images, then the direct product X1×X2X_{1}\times X_{2} is an AA-image.

  3. c)

    An irreducible curve CC is an AA-image if and only if the normalization of CC is ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} or 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}. In these cases CC is an image of the line 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}.

It is useful to observe that an affine variety XX is an AA-image if and only if the algebra of regular functions 𝕂⁡[X]\mathbb{K}[X] can be embedded into some polynomial algebra 𝕂⁡[x1,…,xm]\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}] is such a way that any proper ideal in 𝕂⁡[X]\mathbb{K}[X] generates a proper ideal in 𝕂⁡[x1,…,xm]\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}].

It was observed by the referee that the concept of an AA-image is natural in the context of the famous Zariski Cancellation problem, which asks whether an affine variety XX such that the direct product X×𝔸kX\times\mathbb{A}^{k} is isomorphic to the affine space 𝔸m\mathbb{A}^{m} is necessarily isomorphic to the affine space 𝔸m−k\mathbb{A}^{m-k}. Any potentional counterexample to this problem is an affine variety, which is non-isomorphic to an affine space and is an image of 𝔸m\mathbb{A}^{m} under the projection to the first component in the direct product decomposition.

Let us mention one geometric property that all AA-images have. It is well known that for any m≥2m\geq 2, any positive integer kk and any two kk-tuples of pairwise distinct points on 𝔸m\mathbb{A}^{m} there is an automorphism of 𝔸m\mathbb{A}^{m} which sends the first tuple to the second one. This implies that for any finite subset FF in 𝔸m\mathbb{A}^{m} there is a curve CC in 𝔸m\mathbb{A}^{m} isomorphic to 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1} that contains FF; cf. [2, Corollary 4.18]. We conclude that every AA-image XX is a strongly 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-connected variety, i.e., for every finite subset FF in XX there is a morphism 𝔸1→X\mathbb{A}^{1}\to X whose image contains FF. At the same time it is known that for any finine subset FF in a complete unirational variety XX there exists a moprhism from ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} (and thus from 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}) to XX, whose image contains FF; see [18, IV.3.9].

Now we come to a central concept of this note. Denote by 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a} the additive group (𝕂,+)(\mathbb{K},+) of the ground field. Any nontrivial regular action 𝔾a×X→X\mathbb{G}_{a}\times X\to X on an algebraic variety XX gives rise to a subgroup HH in the automorphism group Aut⁡(X)\mathrm{Aut}(X), which we call a 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-subgroup. Let SAut⁡(X)\mathrm{SAut}(X) be the subgroup in Aut⁡(X)\mathrm{Aut}(X) generated by all 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-subgroups.

Definition 2.

An irreducible variety XX is called very flexible if the group SAut⁡(X)\mathrm{SAut}(X) acts on XX transitively.

Any very flexible variety is smooth. By [2, Theorem 0.1], [3, Theorem 2], and [9, Theorem 1.11], for a smooth quasi-affine variety the condition to be very flexible is equivalent to flexibility in the sence of definitions given in these papers.

Proposition 1.

[2, Proposition 1.4] Let XX be a very flexible variety. Then there are (not necessarily distinct) 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-subgroups H1,…,HmH_{1},\ldots,H_{m} in Aut⁡(X)\mathrm{Aut}(X) such that

X=(H1⋅…⋅Hm).xX=(H_{1}\cdot\ldots\cdot H_{m}).x

for any point x∈Xx\in X.

The next proposition is borrowed from [2, Corollary 1.11].

Proposition 2.

Every very flexible variety is an AA-image.

Proof.

Fix a point x∈Xx\in X and take a sequence of 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-subgroups H1,…,HmH_{1},\ldots,H_{m} as in Proposition 1. Then the map

H1×…×Hm→(H1⋅…⋅Hm).x,(h1,…,hm)↦h1​…​hm.xH_{1}\times\ldots\times H_{m}\to(H_{1}\cdot\ldots\cdot H_{m}).x,\quad(h_{1},\ldots,h_{m})\mapsto h_{1}\ldots h_{m}.x

is a surjective morphism from 𝔸m\mathbb{A}^{m} to XX. ∎

Below we show that Proposition 2 allows to realize many varieties as AA-images. The next result follows directly from [9, Theorem 0.1].

Theorem 1.

Let XX be a very flexible quasi-affine variety and Z⊆XZ\subseteq X be a closed subvariety of codimension at least 22. Then the variety X∖ZX\setminus Z is very flexible.

Corollary 1.

Let ZZ be a closed subset in 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} of codimension at least 22. Then the variety 𝔸n∖Z\mathbb{A}^{n}\setminus Z is very flexible.

2. Three classes of AA-images

2.1. Toric varieties

Let TT be an algebraic torus. A normal irreducible variety X is called toric, if there is a faithful action of TT on XX with an open orbit. We refer to [7, 11] for a systematic theory of toric variety.

A toric variety XX is called degenerate if it is isomorphic to a direct product Y×𝕂×Y\times\mathbb{K}^{\times} for some toric variety YY. By [7, Proposition 3.3.9], a toric variety XX is degenerate if and only if there exists a non-constant invertible regular function on XX. It is easy to see that any toric variety XX is isomorphic to a direct product X′×(𝕂×)kX^{\prime}\times(\mathbb{K}^{\times})^{k} for some non-negative integer kk, where X′X^{\prime} is a non-degenerate toric variety. Clearly, a toric variety can be an AA-image only if XX is non-degenerate.

Theorem A.

A toric variety XX is an AA-image if and only if XX is non-degenerate.

Proof.

It remains to prove that a non-degenerate toric variety XX is an AA-image. By [6, Theorem 2.1], the variety XX can be realized as a good quotient by an action of a diagonalizable group on the open subset 𝔸l∖Z\mathbb{A}^{l}\setminus Z, where ZZ is (maybe empty) union of some coordinate planes of codimension at least 22 in 𝔸l\mathbb{A}^{l}. By Corollary 1, the variety 𝔸l∖Z\mathbb{A}^{l}\setminus Z is an AA-image. So XX is an AA-image as well. ∎

Remark 2.

It follows from [10, Theorem 1.6] that for every compact smooth complex toric variety XX of dimension nn there exists a surjective morpshim φ:ℂn→X\varphi\colon\mathbb{C}^{n}\to X. The proof is based on an algebraic version of a theory of subelliptic manifolds. The technique used in this work is new to us, and we failed to construct explicitly the corresponding surjective morphisms. But this result motivated us to write the present note.

2.2. AA-covered varieties

Let us recall from [3, Definition 4] that an irreducible algebraic variety XX is said to be AA-covered if there is an open covering X=U1∪…∪UrX=U_{1}\cup\ldots\cup U_{r}, where every chart UiU_{i} is isomorphic to the affine space 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n}. The class of AA-covered varieties includes smooth complete spherical varieties, smooth projective rational surfaces, smooth complete rational varieties with a torus action of complexity 1, and many other varieties; see [3, Section 4].

Let us give non-tivial examples of affine AA-covered varieties.

Example 3.

Fix an integer k≥1k\geq 1 and consider the surface X=V⁡(x12−x2k​x3−1)X=V(x_{1}^{2}-x_{2}^{k}x_{3}-1) in 𝔸3\mathbb{A}^{3}. Take the divisor D+D^{+} on XX given by x1=1,x2=0x_{1}=1,x_{2}=0 and the divisor D−D^{-} on XX given by x1=−1,x2=0x_{1}=-1,x_{2}=0. Clearly, D+D^{+} and D−D^{-} have empty intersection. The subset U+:=X∖D+U^{+}:=X\setminus D^{+} is the complement to a divisor on a smooth affine variety, so U+U^{+} is affine; see [22, Lemma 3.3]. Similarly, the open subset U−:=X∖D−U^{-}:=X\setminus D^{-} is affine as well.

Consider the rational function

f=x3x1−1=x1+1x2k.f=\frac{x_{3}}{x_{1}-1}=\frac{x_{1}+1}{x_{2}^{k}}.

It is clear that ff is regular on U+U^{+} and x1=x2k​f−1x_{1}=x_{2}^{k}f-1, x3=(x1−1)​fx_{3}=(x_{1}-1)f. It follows that the algebra of regular functions 𝕂⁡[U+]\mathbb{K}[U^{+}] is the polynomial algebra with generators x2x_{2} and ff. Similarly, the algebra 𝕂⁡[U−]\mathbb{K}[U^{-}] is the polynomial algebra with generators x2x_{2} and gg, where

g=x3x1+1=x1−1x2k.g=\frac{x_{3}}{x_{1}+1}=\frac{x_{1}-1}{x_{2}^{k}}.

We conclude that XX is covered by two open charts U+U^{+} and U−U^{-} each isomorphic to 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}. So the surface XX is AA-covered and is not isomorphic to 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}.

Remark 3.

The referee drew our attention to the fact that the idea of the computation performed in the above example is contained in the unpublished work [8]. Moreover, the referee proposed the following generalization of this construction. Let XX be a smooth affine surface endowed with a smooth surjective 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration φ:X→𝔸1\varphi\colon X\to\mathbb{A}^{1}. Miyanishi proved that every scheme-theoretic fiber of φ\varphi, which is not isomorphic to 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}, decomposes as a disjoint union of curves all isomorphic to 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}. Removing from each such fiber all such curves but one, we obtain an open affine subset in XX with a smooth surjective 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration over 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1} with irreducible fibers. By [17, Theorem 1], such an affine open subset is isomorphic to 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}. We conclude that the surface XX is AA-covered.

Theorem B.

Every AA-covered variety is an AA-image.

Proof.

By [3, Theorem 3], an AA-covered variety XX is a geometric quotient of a very fllexible quasi-affine variety by an action of a torus. So the claim follows from Proposition 2. ∎

Corollary 2.

Every complete rational surface is an AA-image.

Proof.

Passing to normalization and desingularization, we may assume that we deal with a smooth projective rational surface. The latter is AA-covered; see [3, Section 4]. ∎

2.3. Homogeneous spaces

Let XX be a homogeneous space G/HG/H, where GG is a connected linear algebraic group and HH is a closed subgroup in GG.

Theorem C.

A homogeneous space XX is an AA-image if and only if 𝕂​[X]×=𝕂×\mathbb{K}[X]^{\times}=\mathbb{K}^{\times}.

Proof.

We already know that an AA-image has no non-constant invertible regular function. Conversely, assume that 𝕂​[X]×=𝕂×\mathbb{K}[X]^{\times}=\mathbb{K}^{\times}. By [4, Lemma 5.1], in this case the variety XX is homogeneous with respect to the subgroup GsG^{\text{s}} in GG, which is a semidirect product of a maximal semisimple subgroup and the unipotent radical of GG. Since the group GsG^{\text{s}} is generated by 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-subgroups (see, e.g., [23, Lemma 1.1]), we conclude that XX is very flexible and hence is an AA-image. ∎

Remark 4.

Since a homogeneous space of the group SL⁡(V)\mathrm{SL}(V) need not be rational (see, e.g., [23, Example 1.22]), we conclude that an AA-image is not always rational.

Corollary 3.

There is a quasi-affine AA-image XX with a non-finitely generated algebra of regular functions 𝕂⁡[X]\mathbb{K}[X].

Proof.

Let H⊆GL⁡(V)H\subseteq\mathrm{GL}(V) be a unipotent subgroup such that the algebra of invariants 𝕂​[V]H\mathbb{K}[V]^{H} is not finitely generated. Examples of such subgroups are known since the work of Nagata [21]; they provide counterexamples to Hilbert’s Fourteenth Problem. It is proved in [12] that in this case the algebra of regular functions on the quasi-affine homogeneous space X:=SL⁡(V)/HX:=\mathrm{SL}(V)/H is not finitely generated, while Theorem C implies that XX is an AA-image. ∎

3. Concluding remarks and problems

We say that a morphism π:X′→X\pi\colon X^{\prime}\to X of irreducible algebraic varieties does not contract divisors if the image in XX of any prime divisor DD on X′X^{\prime} is not contained in a closed subvariety of codimension 22 in XX.

Proposition 3.

Let π:X′→X\pi\colon X^{\prime}\to X be a surjective morphism of irreducible varieties which does not contract divisors and the variety X′X^{\prime} be quasi-affine and very flexible. If Y⊆XY\subseteq X is a closed subvariety of codimension at least 22, then the complement X∖YX\setminus Y is an AA-image.

Proof.

By assumptions, the preimage π−1​(Y)\pi^{-1}(Y) does not contain divisors on X′X^{\prime}. By Theorem 1, the variety X′∖π−1​(Y)X^{\prime}\setminus\pi^{-1}(Y) is very flexible and hence is an AA-image. So X∖YX\setminus Y is an AA-image as the image of X′∖π−1​(Y)X^{\prime}\setminus\pi^{-1}(Y) under the restriction of the morphism π\pi. ∎

Remark 5.

Note that Proposition 3 is applicable to varieties from Theorems A-C. More precisely, for a non-degenerate toric variety XX the good quotient π:𝔸l∖Z→X\pi\colon\mathbb{A}^{l}\setminus Z\to X does not contract divisors by [1, Proposition 1.6.1.6.(ii)] and the variety 𝔸l∖Z\mathbb{A}^{l}\setminus Z is very flexible by Corollary 1. For AA-covered varieties, the desired morphism π:X′→X\pi\colon X^{\prime}\to X is provided by [3, Theorem 3]. Finally, for a homogeneous space G/HG/H such that the subgroup GsG^{\text{s}} in GG acts on G/HG/H transitively, the orbit map π:Gs→G/H\pi\colon G^{\text{s}}\to G/H is surjective, fibers of this morphism are pairwise isomorphic, so it does not contract divisors, and the variety GsG^{\text{s}} is affine and very flexible.

Continuing the line of Corollary 3 with exotic examples of AA-images, we prove the following result.

Proposition 4.

There exists a three-dimensional complete AA-image XX that is not embeddable into any toric variety.

Proof.

It is proved in [27, Theorem A] that an irreducible normal variety XX admits a closed embedding into a toric variety if and only if every pair of points on XX is contained in a common affine neighborhood. In [25, Example 6.4] the author constructs a good quotient U→XU\to X by an action of a one-dimensional torus TT, where UU is an open subset in the Grassmannian Gr⁡(4,2)\mathrm{Gr}(4,2), the quotient space XX is complete, and there are two points on XX which are not contained in a common affine neighborhood. It follows that XX is three-dimensinal and it is not embeddable into any toric variety.

It is clear from the construction in [25, Example 6.4] that the complement Gr⁡(4,2)∖U\mathrm{Gr}(4,2)\setminus U has codimension at least 22 in Gr⁡(4,2)\mathrm{Gr}(4,2). Since the Grassmannian Gr⁡(4,2)\mathrm{Gr}(4,2) is a homogeneous space of the group SL4\mathrm{SL}_{4}, Theorem C and Proposition 3 imply that XX is an AA-image. ∎

Corollary 4.

An AA-image need not be quasiprojective.

Now we would like to formulate some problems related to the subject of this note.

Problem 1.

Find necessary and sufficient conditions for an algebraic variety XX to be an AA-image.

One can also put a more special problem.

Problem 2.

Characterize nn-dimensional algebraic varieties XX such that there exists a surjective morphism φ:𝔸n→X\varphi\colon\mathbb{A}^{n}\to X.

In fact, we have no example of an nn-dimensional AA-image XX such that there is no surjective morphism φ:𝔸n→X\varphi\colon\mathbb{A}^{n}\to X. In particular, a variety XX in Problem 2 need not be rational: there are examples of quotient spaces X=𝔸n//HX=\mathbb{A}^{n}/\!/H, where HH is a finite group and XX is not rational; see [24, Theorem 3.6].

Remark 6.

In the preliminary version of this note we also asked whether for any irreducible algebraic variety XX there exists a surjective morphism ϕ:V→X\phi\colon V\to X from an irreducible affine variety VV. The referee informed us that the answer to this question is positive. Namely, Jouanolou [15] proved that every quasi-projective variety XX admits a vector bundle torsor V→XV\to X with affine total space VV. This result was extended by Thomason (see [26]) to a wider class of algebraic varieties including all smooth algebraic varieties. Applying Hironaka’s desingularization theorem, we obtain a desingularization X~→X\widetilde{X}\to X and then use Jouanolou-Thomason’s construction V~→X~\widetilde{V}\to\widetilde{X} to get a surjection V~→X\widetilde{V}\to X. Moreover, the referee observed that XX is an AA-image if and only if any affine variety V~\widetilde{V} obtained this way is an AA-image.

The next question asks whether we may use AA-images as ambient spaces for arbitrary algebraic varieties, just as affine (projective) spaces serve for affine (projective) varieties.

Problem 3.

Let XX be an algebraic variety. Is it possible to realize XX as a closed subvariety in some AA-image X~\widetilde{X}?

Finally, let us consider an even more general situation. It is well known that the image of a morphism φ:X1→X2\varphi\colon X_{1}\to X_{2} of algebraic varieties need not be a subvariety in X2X_{2}. By Chevalley’s theorem, the image of a morphism is a constructible subset of X2X_{2}, i.e., a finite disjoint union of locally closed subvarieties in X2X_{2}; see [13, Theorem I.4.4].

Problem 4.

Let WW be an irreducible constructible subset of an algebraic variety X2X_{2}. Do there exist an irreducible algebraic variety X1X_{1} and a morphism φ:X1→X2\varphi\colon X_{1}\to X_{2} such that the image of φ\varphi coincides with WW?

Remark 7.

After a preprint version of this note appeared in September, 2022, three more works [5, 16, 19] with new results on AA-images became available.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
